claim: The activity of Src-family kinases (SFKs), which phosphorylate immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs), is a critical factor regulating myeloid-cell activation.
source: The activity of Src-family kinases (SFKs), which phosphorylate immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs), is a critical factor regulating myeloid-cell activation.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about SFK function in myeloid cells.

claim: The SFK LynA is uniquely susceptible to rapid ubiquitin-mediated degradation in macrophages.
source: We reported previously that the SFK LynA is uniquely susceptible to rapid ubiquitin-mediated degradation in macrophages, functioning as a rheostat regulating signaling (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: LynA functions as a rheostat regulating signaling in macrophages.
source: We reported previously that the SFK LynA is uniquely susceptible to rapid ubiquitin-mediated degradation in macrophages, functioning as a rheostat regulating signaling (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl preferentially targets LynA via a phosphorylated tyrosine (Y32) in its unique region.
source: Using genetic, biochemical, and quantitative phosphopeptide analyses, we found that the E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl preferentially targets LynA via a phosphorylated tyrosine (Y32) in its unique region.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic, biochemical, and mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: c-Cbl recognition of phosphorylated Y32 in LynA depresses steady-state expression of LynA in macrophages derived from mice.
source: This distinct mode of c-Cbl recognition depresses steady-state expression of LynA in macrophages derived from mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing LynA expression in wild-type and c-Cbl knockout macrophages.

claim: Mast cells express little c-Cbl.
source: Mast cells, however, express little c-Cbl and have correspondingly high LynA.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data and RNAseq data from the Immunological Genome Project.

claim: Mast cells have correspondingly high LynA protein levels.
source: Mast cells, however, express little c-Cbl and have correspondingly high LynA.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data comparing LynA levels in mast cells and macrophages.

claim: Upon activation, mast-cell LynA is not rapidly degraded.
source: Upon activation, mast-cell LynA is not rapidly degraded, and SFK-mediated signaling is amplified relative to macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course immunoblot data showing LynA stability in 3-IB-PP1-treated mast cells.

claim: SFK-mediated signaling is amplified in mast cells relative to macrophages.
source: Upon activation, mast-cell LynA is not rapidly degraded, and SFK-mediated signaling is amplified relative to macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing enhanced Erk phosphorylation in mast cells compared to macrophages.

claim: Cell-specific c-Cbl expression builds cell specificity into the LynA checkpoint.
source: Cell-specific c-Cbl expression thus builds cell specificity into the LynA checkpoint.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data from macrophages and mast cells showing differential c-Cbl expression and LynA regulation.

claim: Phosphorylation of immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) by Src-family kinases (SFKs) is the first enzymatic step in the activation of an innate immune response during a pathogen encounter.
source: Phosphorylation of immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) by Src-family kinases (SFKs) is the first enzymatic step in the activation of an innate immune response during a pathogen encounter.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ITAM signaling pathways.

claim: Initiation of cell-activating signaling typically occurs within clusters of ITAM-coupled receptors such as FcγR or the hemi-ITAM Dectin-1.
source: Initiation of cell-activating signaling typically occurs within clusters of ITAM-coupled receptors such as FcγR (Guilliams et al., 2014) or the hemi-ITAM Dectin-1 (Brown, 2006; Deng et al., 2015), nucleated by highly multivalent immunoglobulin-G-decorated pathogens or fungal cell-wall β-glucans, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SFKs and phosphorylated ITAMs trigger activation of the tyrosine kinase Syk.
source: Together, SFKs and phosphorylated ITAMs trigger activation of the tyrosine kinase Syk (Lowell, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The SFKs and Syk drive activation of membrane-proximal signaling through adaptor proteins, cytoskeleton-modulating proteins, and Tec kinases.
source: The SFKs and Syk then drive activation of membrane-proximal signaling through adaptor proteins; cytoskeleton-modulating proteins, such as the FAK/Pyk2 kinases and Paxillin; and Tec kinases, which activate second-messenger pathways via phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and phospholipases Cγ (PLCγ1/2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Early ITAM signaling events ultimately lead to downstream signaling through Erk1/2 and other pathways.
source: These early events ultimately lead to downstream signaling through Erk1/2 and other pathways (Lowell, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The responsiveness of innate immune cells is tightly regulated.
source: As the byproducts of activated macrophages can be toxic (e.g. release of reactive oxygen species) and drive inflammation (e.g. release of tumor necrosis factor α), the responsiveness of innate immune cells is tightly regulated (Goodridge et al., 2011; Takai, 2002; Sondermann, 2016; Chiffoleau, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by phosphatases CD45 and CD148.
source: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by the phosphatases CD45 and CD148 (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Bakalar et al., 2018), cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion (Jaumouillé et al., 2014), signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Abram and Lowell, 2008) and inhibitory ITAMs (Hamerman and Lanier, 2006; Hamerman et al., 2009), and degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases (Lutz-Nicoladoni et al., 2015; Liyasova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion contribute to tuning the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells.
source: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by the phosphatases CD45 and CD148 (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Bakalar et al., 2018), cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion (Jaumouillé et al., 2014), signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Abram and Lowell, 2008) and inhibitory ITAMs (Hamerman and Lanier, 2006; Hamerman et al., 2009), and degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases (Lutz-Nicoladoni et al., 2015; Liyasova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) and inhibitory ITAMs contributes to tuning the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells.
source: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by the phosphatases CD45 and CD148 (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Bakalar et al., 2018), cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion (Jaumouillé et al., 2014), signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Abram and Lowell, 2008) and inhibitory ITAMs (Hamerman and Lanier, 2006; Hamerman et al., 2009), and degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases (Lutz-Nicoladoni et al., 2015; Liyasova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases contributes to tuning the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells.
source: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by the phosphatases CD45 and CD148 (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Bakalar et al., 2018), cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion (Jaumouillé et al., 2014), signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Abram and Lowell, 2008) and inhibitory ITAMs (Hamerman and Lanier, 2006; Hamerman et al., 2009), and degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases (Lutz-Nicoladoni et al., 2015; Liyasova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In myeloid cells, SFKs typically include Fgr, Fyn, two isoforms of Hck, and two splice forms of Lyn.
source: The SFKs, which in myeloid cells typically include Fgr, Fyn, two isoforms of Hck, and two splice forms of Lyn, may also have positive and negative functions (Abram and Lowell, 2008; Mkaddem et al., 2017; Alvarez-Errico et al., 2010; Scapini et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SFKs may have positive and negative functions in myeloid cells.
source: The SFKs, which in myeloid cells typically include Fgr, Fyn, two isoforms of Hck, and two splice forms of Lyn, may also have positive and negative functions (Abram and Lowell, 2008; Mkaddem et al., 2017; Alvarez-Errico et al., 2010; Scapini et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activated LynA is rapidly and specifically targeted for polyubiquitination and degradation, forming the basis of a signaling checkpoint that blocks spurious macrophage activation.
source: Layered onto the traditional positive- and negative-regulatory roles of the SFKs, activated LynA (the longer of the two Lyn splice forms) is rapidly and specifically targeted for polyubiquitination and degradation, forming the basis of a signaling checkpoint that blocks spurious macrophage activation (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The LynA checkpoint can be bypassed when LynA is upregulated, with LynA acting as a rheostat to tune macrophage sensitivity.
source: This checkpoint can be bypassed when LynA is upregulated, with LynA acting as a rheostat to tune macrophage sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LynA is transcriptionally upregulated when macrophages are treated with interferon (IFN)-γ.
source: For instance, LynA is transcriptionally upregulated when macrophages are treated with interferon (IFN)-γ, and these primed cells have a lower threshold for SFK-mediated signaling (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IFN-γ-primed macrophages have a lower threshold for SFK-mediated signaling.
source: For instance, LynA is transcriptionally upregulated when macrophages are treated with interferon (IFN)-γ, and these primed cells have a lower threshold for SFK-mediated signaling (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The molecular mechanism that selectively targets LynA for polyubiquitination has not been elucidated previously.
source: The molecular mechanism that selectively targets LynA for polyubiquitination has not been elucidated previously.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current work.

claim: Dectin-1 and FcγR signaling pathways in macrophages are typically triggered in the context of pathogen-induced µm-scale clusters of receptors.
source: Unlike Dectin-1 and FcγR signaling pathways in macrophages, which are typically triggered in the context of pathogen-induced µm-scale clusters of receptors (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Freedman et al., 2015), mast-cell FcεR signaling has a low threshold for activation; small or even monovalent antigen-IgE complexes can induce a signaling response in the context of a cell-particle interaction (Andrews et al., 2009; Felce et al., 2018; Carroll-Portillo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mast-cell FcεR signaling has a low threshold for activation.
source: Unlike Dectin-1 and FcγR signaling pathways in macrophages, which are typically triggered in the context of pathogen-induced µm-scale clusters of receptors (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Freedman et al., 2015), mast-cell FcεR signaling has a low threshold for activation; small or even monovalent antigen-IgE complexes can induce a signaling response in the context of a cell-particle interaction (Andrews et al., 2009; Felce et al., 2018; Carroll-Portillo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Small or even monovalent antigen-IgE complexes can induce a signaling response in mast cells in the context of a cell-particle interaction.
source: Unlike Dectin-1 and FcγR signaling pathways in macrophages, which are typically triggered in the context of pathogen-induced µm-scale clusters of receptors (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Freedman et al., 2015), mast-cell FcεR signaling has a low threshold for activation; small or even monovalent antigen-IgE complexes can induce a signaling response in the context of a cell-particle interaction (Andrews et al., 2009; Felce et al., 2018; Carroll-Portillo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The binding dynamics of Syk with FcεRI in mast cells is unaffected by the size of receptor aggregates.
source: Supporting this more permissive signaling function, the binding dynamics of Syk with FcεRI in mast cells is unaffected by the size of receptor aggregates (Schwartz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mast cells express LynA.
source: Like macrophages, mast cells express LynA, and the disparity in the receptor sensitivity of these two cell types has not previously been explained.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about mast cell protein expression.

claim: The disparity in the receptor sensitivity of macrophages and mast cells has not previously been explained.
source: Like macrophages, mast cells express LynA, and the disparity in the receptor sensitivity of these two cell types has not previously been explained.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current work.

claim: 3-IB-PP1 specifically inhibits a variant of the SFK-inhibitory kinase Csk (CskAS).
source: To reveal the requirements for LynA degradation, we synchronized receptor-independent SFK activation using the designer inhibitor 3-IB-PP1 (Okuzumi et al., 2010; Okuzumi et al., 2009; Schoenborn et al., 2011), which specifically inhibits a variant of the SFK-inhibitory kinase Csk (CskAS) (Freedman et al., 2015; Schoenborn et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Csk is responsible for phosphorylating a key inhibitory tyrosine in the C-terminal tail of all the SFKs.
source: Csk is responsible for phosphorylating a key inhibitory tyrosine in the C-terminal tail of all the SFKs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Csk function.

claim: Inhibiting CskAS with 3-IB-PP1 disrupts the dynamic equilibrium between Csk and the phosphatases CD45 and CD148, leading to rapid and robust SFK activation.
source: Inhibiting CskAS with 3-IB-PP1 disrupts the dynamic equilibrium between Csk and the phosphatases CD45 and CD148, which dephosphorylate the inhibitory tyrosine, leading to rapid and robust SFK activation (Chow and Veillette, 1995; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 3-IB-PP1-induced SFK activation leads to the phosphorylation and likely activation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl.
source: 3-IB-PP1-induced SFK activation leads to the phosphorylation and likely activation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl (Feshchenko et al., 1998; Dou et al., 2012; Freedman et al., 2015) and the preferential polyubiquitination and degradation of LynA in macrophages (Freedman et al., 2015), but it was not clear whether these two events were linked.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 3-IB-PP1-induced SFK activation leads to the preferential polyubiquitination and degradation of LynA in macrophages.
source: 3-IB-PP1-induced SFK activation leads to the phosphorylation and likely activation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl (Feshchenko et al., 1998; Dou et al., 2012; Freedman et al., 2015) and the preferential polyubiquitination and degradation of LynA in macrophages (Freedman et al., 2015), but it was not clear whether these two events were linked.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: c-Cbl mediates rapid degradation of LynA upon activation in macrophages.
source: Using knockout and overexpression models coupled with analyses of protein abundance and cell signaling, we now demonstrate that c-Cbl controls the steady-state expression of LynA and mediates its rapid degradation upon activation in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from c-Cbl knockout experiments showing impaired LynA degradation.

claim: LynA is targeted by c-Cbl in response to phosphorylation of tyrosine 32 (Y32) within the LynA unique region.
source: Quantitative targeted mass spectrometry shows that LynA is targeted by c-Cbl in response to phosphorylation of tyrosine 32 (Y32) within the LynA unique region, a process mediated by LynA, LynB or the shorter isoform of Hck.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing Y32 phosphorylation and mutagenesis data showing Y32 is required for degradation.

claim: Phosphorylation of LynA Y32 is mediated by LynA, LynB or the shorter isoform of Hck.
source: Quantitative targeted mass spectrometry shows that LynA is targeted by c-Cbl in response to phosphorylation of tyrosine 32 (Y32) within the LynA unique region, a process mediated by LynA, LynB or the shorter isoform of Hck.
evidence: This claim is supported by cotransfection experiments showing which SFKs can induce LynA degradation in trans.

claim: The c-Cbl recognition mode for LynA via Y32 is distinct from the slower-phase action of c-Cbl and other E3 ligases on LynB and the other SFKs.
source: This recognition mode is distinct from the slower-phase action of c-Cbl and other E3 ligases on LynB and the other SFKs (Freedman et al., 2015; Sanjay et al., 2001; Sanjay et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing differential degradation kinetics and by citations to prior literature.

claim: The LynA checkpoint is cell-specific.
source: Finally, we have discovered that the LynA checkpoint is cell-specific.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data from macrophages and mast cells.

claim: Mast cells express very little c-Cbl but abundant Cbl-b.
source: In mast cells, which express very little c-Cbl but abundant Cbl-b, LynA is not rapidly degraded upon activation, a function that can be rescued by induced overexpression of c-Cbl.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data comparing c-Cbl and Cbl-b levels in mast cells and macrophages.

claim: Rapid degradation of LynA in mast cells can be rescued by induced overexpression of c-Cbl.
source: In mast cells, which express very little c-Cbl but abundant Cbl-b, LynA is not rapidly degraded upon activation, a function that can be rescued by induced overexpression of c-Cbl.
evidence: This claim is supported by saRNA experiments showing that increasing c-Cbl expression in mast cells induces LynA degradation.

claim: The differential regulation of c-Cbl and LynA may drive mast cells toward a lower activation threshold than macrophages.
source: The differential regulation of c-Cbl and LynA may drive mast cells toward a lower activation threshold than macrophages.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing differential c-Cbl expression and LynA stability in mast cells versus macrophages.

claim: Knockout of c-Cbl profoundly impaired the degradation of activated LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Knockout of c-Cbl profoundly impaired the degradation of activated LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment, with LynA levels remaining at 100% after 1 min of exposure to 3-IB-PP1 in CskASc-CblKO BMDMs compared to 60% in CskAS BMDMs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by densitometry quantification of immunoblots shown in Figure 1.

claim: CskASc-CblKO BMDMs expressed 3-fold more LynA protein than CskAS at steady state.
source: CskASc-CblKO BMDMs also expressed 3-fold more LynA protein than CskAS at steady state (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by densitometry quantification of immunoblots shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cbl-b does not have a role in suppressing the steady-state level or promoting the activation-induced degradation of LynA.
source: Although it has been reported previously that c-Cbl and Cbl-b have some redundant functions (Naramura et al., 2002; Purev et al., 2009), we were unable to detect any role for Cbl-b in suppressing the steady-state level or promoting the activation-induced degradation of LynA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Cbl-b knockout experiments showing no effect on LynA degradation.

claim: Upon treatment for 1 min with 3-IB-PP1, LynA was 81% reduced in CskASCbl-bKO compared to 60% in CskAS BMDMs.
source: Upon treatment for 1 min with 3-IB-PP1, LynA was 81% reduced in CskASCbl-bKO compared to 60% in CskAS BMDMs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by densitometry quantification of immunoblots shown in Figure 1.

claim: CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs show a compensatory upregulation of c-Cbl protein expression.
source: This increase in LynA degradation may be explained by a compensatory upregulation of c-Cbl protein expression in CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Syk phosphorylation is enhanced in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASc-CblKO BMDMs.
source: Notably, Syk phosphorylation is enhanced in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASc-CblKO BMDMs, consistent with the higher expression level and longer half-life of LynA protein (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Syk phosphorylation is enhanced in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs, likely due to the direct role of Cbl-b on Syk inhibition.
source: Syk phosphorylation is also enhanced in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs, but this is likely due to the direct role of Cbl-b on Syk inhibition (Sohn et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data and citation to prior literature.

claim: Erk phosphorylation in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASc-CblKO BMDMs is impaired, likely due to the loss of the adaptor function of c-Cbl in PI3K signaling.
source: Erk phosphorylation in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASc-CblKO BMDMs is impaired (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), likely due to the loss of the adaptor function of c-Cbl in PI3K signaling (Ueno et al., 1998; Hunter et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior literature.

claim: In 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs, Erk1/2 phosphorylation is enhanced, likely due to the negative-regulatory role of Cbl-b for Syk and other upstream signaling intermediates.
source: In 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs, Erk1/2 phosphorylation, like Syk phosphorylation, is enhanced, again likely due to the negative-regulatory role of Cbl-b for Syk and other upstream signaling intermediates.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data and inference from known Cbl-b functions.

claim: siRNA knockdown of c-Cbl resulted in modest but specific knockdown (70% reduced).
source: Immunoblots of siRNA-transfected BMDM lysates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) showed modest but specific knockdown of c-Cbl (70% reduced) and Cbl-b (60% reduced), importantly, without a corresponding increase in c-Cbl expression as a consequence of Cbl-b knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: siRNA knockdown of Cbl-b resulted in modest but specific knockdown (60% reduced).
source: Immunoblots of siRNA-transfected BMDM lysates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) showed modest but specific knockdown of c-Cbl (70% reduced) and Cbl-b (60% reduced), importantly, without a corresponding increase in c-Cbl expression as a consequence of Cbl-b knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of c-Cbl but not Cbl-b resulted in impaired degradation of LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment in siRNA experiments.
source: As in the knockout models, loss of c-Cbl but not Cbl-b resulted in impaired degradation of LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment and increased steady-state expression of LynA protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from siRNA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of c-Cbl but not Cbl-b resulted in increased steady-state expression of LynA protein in siRNA experiments.
source: As in the knockout models, loss of c-Cbl but not Cbl-b resulted in impaired degradation of LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment and increased steady-state expression of LynA protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from siRNA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Without c-Cbl upregulation in Cbl-b-knockdown BMDMs, there was no increase in the LynA degradation efficiency or decrease in the steady-state level of LynA protein.
source: Without c-Cbl upregulation in Cbl-b-knockdown BMDMs, there was no increase in the LynA degradation efficiency or decrease in the steady-state level of LynA protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D), supporting our hypothesis that this observation in CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs was c-Cbl-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from siRNA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: c-Cbl is solely responsible for the rapid and specific degradation of LynA.
source: Overall, we conclude that c-Cbl is solely responsible for the rapid and specific degradation of LynA, whereas other E3 ubiquitin ligases can complement the canonical SFK-binding and -polyubiquitinating function of c-Cbl (Sanjay et al., 2001; Sanjay et al., 2006), which mediates slower degradation of LynA and the other SFKs (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from knockout and siRNA experiments and citations to prior literature.

claim: Other E3 ubiquitin ligases can complement the canonical SFK-binding and -polyubiquitinating function of c-Cbl, which mediates slower degradation of LynA and the other SFKs.
source: Overall, we conclude that c-Cbl is solely responsible for the rapid and specific degradation of LynA, whereas other E3 ubiquitin ligases can complement the canonical SFK-binding and -polyubiquitinating function of c-Cbl (Sanjay et al., 2001; Sanjay et al., 2006), which mediates slower degradation of LynA and the other SFKs (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and inference from the data.

claim: Macrophage Hck, Fgr, and LynB are degraded >10 fold more slowly than LynA during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Susceptibility to rapid, activation-induced degradation differentiates LynA from the splice variant LynB and the other abundant SFKs in macrophages, Hck (59 and 56 kDa transcripts) and Fgr (Scapini et al., 2009), which are degraded >10 fold more slowly than LynA during 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Fyn has been reported to play an important role in macrophage inflammatory signaling.
source: The SFK FynT (Fyn) has also been reported to play an important role in macrophage inflammatory signaling (Mkaddem et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Macrophage Fyn is long-lived during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: We now confirm that, like Hck, Fgr, and LynB, macrophage Fyn is long-lived during 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 2A), although we have been unable to detect Fyn activation in response to 3-IB-PP1 (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fyn activation in response to 3-IB-PP1 in macrophages was not detected.
source: We now confirm that, like Hck, Fgr, and LynB, macrophage Fyn is long-lived during 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 2A), although we have been unable to detect Fyn activation in response to 3-IB-PP1 (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LynA is rapidly degraded in Jurkat cells treated with 3-IB-PP1, in contrast to longer-lived Lck and Fyn.
source: As in macrophages, LynA is rapidly degraded in Jurkat cells treated with 3-IB-PP1, in contrast to longer-lived Lck (Schoenborn et al., 2011) and Fyn (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2B and citation to prior literature.

claim: Cell types that do not express Lyn may lack an analogous, rapid off-switch for SFK signaling.
source: This highlights the unique susceptibility of LynA to rapid, c-Cbl-mediated degradation and suggests that cell types, such as T cells, that do not express Lyn may lack an analogous, rapid off-switch for SFK signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing unique LynA degradation properties.

claim: c-Cbl overexpression in Jurkat cells increased the rate of LynA degradation.
source: As predicted, c-Cbl overexpression in Jurkat cells increased the rate of LynA degradation (30% depletion after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1 in c-Cbl-overexpressing Jurkat cells versus no detectable depletion in either ctrl or Cbl-b-overexpressing cells) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Jurkat cells, which do not normally express Lyn, are capable of supporting rapid, c-Cbl-mediated degradation of LynA.
source: This observation is consistent with the knockout and siRNA experiments in BMDMs, demonstrating that Jurkat cells, which do not normally express Lyn, are capable of supporting rapid, c-Cbl-mediated degradation of LynA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Jurkat cell transfection experiments.

claim: LynB lacks a 21 amino-acid insert found in the unique region of LynA.
source: LynB, which lacks a 21 amino-acid insert found in the unique region of LynA (Figure 3D), was less efficiently degraded (10% depleted after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1) than LynA (40% depleted after 5 min) in c-Cbl- and memCskAS-cotransfected Jurkat cells (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 3D and citation to prior literature.

claim: LynB was less efficiently degraded (10% depleted after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1) than LynA (40% depleted after 5 min) in c-Cbl- and memCskAS-cotransfected Jurkat cells.
source: LynB, which lacks a 21 amino-acid insert found in the unique region of LynA (Figure 3D), was less efficiently degraded (10% depleted after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1) than LynA (40% depleted after 5 min) in c-Cbl- and memCskAS-cotransfected Jurkat cells (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The unique susceptibility of LynA to rapid degradation is preserved in the Jurkat model.
source: Again, these data mirror our findings in CskAS BMDMs (Freedman et al., 2015) and confirm that the unique susceptibility of LynA to rapid degradation is preserved in the Jurkat model.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Jurkat cell experiments and citation to prior work.

claim: The unique-region insert of LynA (residues 23–43) contains a tyrosine residue reported to be phosphorylated in cancer cells (Y32).
source: We hypothesized that the c-Cbl recognition site in LynA must lie within the unique-region insert (residues 23–43), absent in LynB (Yi et al., 1991; Stanley et al., 1991), which contains a tyrosine residue reported to be phosphorylated in cancer cells (Y32; Huang et al., 2013; Tornillo et al., 2018), a predicted threonine phosphorylation site (T27; NetPhos 3.1, Blom et al., 2004) and a predicted lysine ubiquitination site (K40; UbPred, Radivojac et al., 2010) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Substituting tyrosine 32 with either alanine or phenylalanine blocked the rapid degradation of LynA.
source: Substituting tyrosine 32 with either alanine or phenylalanine blocked the rapid degradation of LynA (Figure 3E), reducing the depletion after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1 from 40% (LynA) to 10% (LynAY32A) or 8% (LynAY32F), levels indistinguishable from LynB (10%) (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Substitution of Y32 did not alter the membrane localization of a unique-region construct at steady state or after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Substitution of Y32 did not alter the membrane localization of a unique-region construct at steady state or after 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither the predicted ubiquitination-site mutation (LynAK40R) nor the predicted threonine phosphorylation site mutation (LynAT27A) significantly affected the rate of LynA degradation.
source: Neither the predicted ubiquitination-site mutation (LynAK40R) nor the predicted threonine phosphorylation site mutation (LynAT27A) significantly affected the rate of LynA degradation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: LynB is 2-fold and LynAY32A 3-fold more highly expressed than wild-type LynA at steady state in Jurkat cells.
source: LynB is 2-fold and LynAY32A 3-fold more highly expressed than wild-type LynA, LynAK40R, or LynAT27A at steady state, resulting in 3- to 4-fold more protein remaining after 20 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The unique tyrosine residue Y32 in the LynA insert flags LynA for rapid, c-Cbl-mediated degradation.
source: Overall, we conclude that the unique tyrosine residue Y32 in the LynA insert flags LynA for rapid, c-Cbl-mediated degradation and that this mechanism both determines the half-life of activated LynA protein during signaling and tunes its steady-state expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis data showing Y32 is required for degradation.

claim: The Y32-mediated mechanism determines the half-life of activated LynA protein during signaling and tunes its steady-state expression.
source: Overall, we conclude that the unique tyrosine residue Y32 in the LynA insert flags LynA for rapid, c-Cbl-mediated degradation and that this mechanism both determines the half-life of activated LynA protein during signaling and tunes its steady-state expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing effects of Y32 mutation on both degradation kinetics and steady-state levels.

claim: Phosphorylated LynAY32 has been found in liver and mammary tumor cells.
source: Although phosphorylated LynAY32 has been found in liver and mammary tumor cells (Huang et al., 2013; Tornillo et al., 2018), it has been unclear whether this posttranslational modification is functionally relevant in hematopoietic cells and whether Y32 is phosphorylated as a consequence of SFK activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Quantitative analysis of LynA protein using targeted LC-MS/MS detected phosphorylation at Y32 in BMDMs.
source: To probe for Y32 phosphorylation, we performed quantitative analysis of LynA protein using targeted liquid-chromatography-coupled tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) after immunoprecipitation of LynA from resting and 3-IB-PP1-treated BMDMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: pY32 was 6- to 12-fold enriched in nonubiquitinated LynA from 3-IB-PP1-treated BMDMs relative to resting BMDMs.
source: We detected LynA Y32 phosphorylation in 3-IB-PP1-treated BMDMs in two independent experiments. After immunoprecipitation and sample processing, pY32 was 6- to 12-fold enriched in nonubiquitinated LynA from 3-IB-PP1-treated BMDMs relative to resting BMDMs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: LynA Y32 is a site of inducible phosphorylation following activation of SFKs in primary macrophages.
source: LynA Y32 is therefore a site of inducible phosphorylation following activation of SFKs in primary macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing increased Y32 phosphorylation after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.

claim: In resting BMDMs the vast majority of LynA is inactive and therefore protected from bulk degradation by lack of Y32 phosphorylation.
source: In resting BMDMs the vast majority of LynA is inactive (Freedman et al., 2015) and therefore protected from bulk degradation by lack of Y32 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mass spectrometry data and citation to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylated Y32 peptide was detectable at low levels in resting BMDMs.
source: Phosphorylated Y32 peptide was, however, detectable at low levels in resting BMDMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Phosphorylation of LynA Y32 was 6.0- to 6.4-fold higher in polyubiquitinated LynA than in nonubiquitinated LynA.
source: Although phosphorylation of LynA Y32 was detected in activated, nonubiquitinated LynA, it was 6.0- to 6.4-fold higher in polyubiquitinated LynA (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Phosphorylation of LynA Y32 is an early consequence of SFK activation and a prerequisite for rapid polyubiquitination by c-Cbl.
source: It is therefore likely that phosphorylation of LynA Y32 is an early consequence of SFK activation and a prerequisite for rapid polyubiquitination by c-Cbl.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mass spectrometry data showing enrichment of pY32 in polyubiquitinated LynA.

claim: Syk and FAK are phosphorylated on activating tyrosine residues in CskAS BMDMs treated with 3-IB-PP1.
source: In macrophages and other hematopoietic cells SFKs are the first kinases to be activated upon ITAM-coupled receptor engagement, phosphorylating intracellular ITAMs, ITAM-associated Syk or Zap70 (Yan et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2010), and integrin-associated FAK or Pyk2 (Lowell, 2011; Han et al., 2013). We have reported that Syk and FAK are phosphorylated on activating tyrosine residues in CskAS BMDMs treated with 3-IB-PP1 (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LynA degradation was unaffected by Syk or FAK/Pyk2 inhibition but abrogated by SFK inhibition.
source: LynA degradation was unaffected by Syk or FAK/Pyk2 inhibition but abrogated by SFK inhibition (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neither Syk, FAK, Pyk2 nor any of their downstream targets participate in a negative-feedback loop leading to LynA degradation.
source: Given these data, we conclude that neither Syk, FAK, or Pyk2 nor any of their downstream targets participate in a negative-feedback loop leading to LynA degradation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The SFKs themselves induce LynA degradation.
source: This suggests that the only kinases upstream of Syk, FAK, and Pyk2, the SFKs themselves, induce LynA degradation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from inhibitor experiments.

claim: Only catalytically competent LynA was subject to rapid, 3-IB-PP1-induced degradation in JCaM1.6 cells.
source: When transfected into JCaM1.6 cells along with memCskAS and c-Cbl, only catalytically competent His6V5-tagged LynA was subject to rapid, 3-IB-PP1-induced degradation (Figure 6A); we did not detect degradation of the substrate-binding-impaired variant (T410K) or the activation-loop-mutated variant (Y397F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Activated Lck was unable to induce degradation of LynA in trans in Jurkat cells.
source: Activated Lck, however, was unable to induce degradation of LynA in trans, with no detectable loss of either catalytically-impaired variant (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The active-site mutant LynAK275R was resistant to 3-IB-PP1-induced degradation.
source: To ensure that the substrate-binding and conformational elements altered in the T410K and Y397F variants did not affect our results, we confirmed that the active-site mutant LynAK275R was similarly resistant to 3-IB-PP1-induced degradation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither the Jurkat-cell SFKs (Lck/Fyn) nor the myeloid-cell SFK targets (Syk and FAK/Pyk2) participate in LynA degradation.
source: Observing that neither the Jurkat-cell SFKs (Lck/Fyn) nor the myeloid-cell SFK targets (Syk and FAK/Pyk2) participate in LynA degradation, we turned our focus to the major SFKs in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: LynA provides the sole initiating signal to trigger its own degradation in Jurkat cells cotransfected with c-Cbl and memCskAS.
source: We showed above that wild-type LynA is degraded in 3-IB-PP1-treated Jurkat cells cotransfected with c-Cbl and memCskAS, suggesting that LynA provides the sole initiating signal to trigger its own degradation, in (i) its ability to induce the phosphorylation of LynA Y32 and (ii) its ability to phosphorylate and activate c-Cbl.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from data showing LynA degradation in Jurkat cells.

claim: Wild-type LynA, LynAY32A, and LynB were all capable of inducing the degradation of LynAT410K in trans in JCaM1.6 cells.
source: Cotransfected wild-type LynA, LynAY32A, and LynB were all capable of inducing the degradation of LynAT410K in trans. Where depletion of LynAT410K transfected alone was undetectable after 5 min of 3-IB-PP1 treatment, cotransfected wild-type LynA, LynAY32A, and LynB induced depletion of LynAT410K by 20%, 37%, and 40%, respectively; wild-type LynA alone was depleted by 40% at the same time point (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Expression of Hck from a dual 59 kDa- and 56 kDa-expressing (Hck59+56) plasmid induced depletion of LynAT410K by 17% after a 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1.
source: Expression of Hck from a dual 59 kDa- and 56 kDa-expressing (Hck59+56) plasmid induced depletion of LynAT410K by 17% after a 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Hck59 alone was able to phosphorylate the activation loop of LynAT410K but unable to phosphorylate Zap70 or c-Cbl or induce degradation of LynAT410K.
source: Hck59 alone was able to phosphorylate the activation loop of LynAT410K but unable to phosphorylate Zap70 or c-Cbl or induce degradation of LynAT410K (Figure 7A,B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the dual Hck expression condition only the shorter isoform, Hck56, was responsible for mediating phosphorylation of Zap70 and c-Cbl and degradation of LynA.
source: This suggests that in the dual expression condition only the shorter isoform, Hck56, was responsible for mediating phosphorylation of Zap70 and c-Cbl and degradation of LynA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from data comparing Hck59 alone versus Hck59+56.

claim: Endogenous Fyn in Jurkat cells is not activated during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Endogenous Fyn in Jurkat cells is not activated during 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 7A), and we were unable to increase the expression or 3-IB-PP1-induced activation of Fyn by cotransfection.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: FynB induced activation-loop phosphorylation of LynAT410K but did not phosphorylate Zap70 or c-Cbl or induce LynAT410K degradation.
source: Like Hck59, FynB induced activation-loop phosphorylation of LynAT410K (Figure 7B) but did not phosphorylate Zap70 or c-Cbl or induce LynAT410K degradation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fgr and Lck were capable of inducing Zap70 and c-Cbl phosphorylation but unable to induce degradation of LynAT410K.
source: Although neither was able to induce degradation of LynAT410K, Fgr and Lck were markedly different from Hck59 and FynB in that, in addition to activation-loop-phosphorylating LynAT410K, they were also capable of inducing Zap70 and c-Cbl phosphorylation (Figure 7B,D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The failure of Lck and Fgr to mediate LynA degradation is due to substrate specificity rather than localization or lack of participation in ITAM signaling pathways.
source: Again, this suggests that the failure of Lck and Fgr to mediate LynA degradation is due to substrate specificity rather than localization or lack of participation in ITAM signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from data showing Lck and Fgr can phosphorylate Zap70 and c-Cbl but not induce LynA degradation.

claim: LynA degradation can be induced by SFK activity in trans.
source: Overall, these results show that LynA degradation can be induced by SFK activity in trans.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from cotransfection experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Activated LynA, LynB, and Hck56 can all mediate LynA degradation to some extent, but Lyn appears to do this most efficiently.
source: Activated LynA, LynB, and Hck56 can all mediate LynA degradation to some extent, but Lyn appears to do this most efficiently, due either to faster activation kinetics or more efficient phosphorylation of LynA and c-Cbl.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from data comparing different SFKs' abilities to induce LynA degradation.

claim: Mast cells express very low levels of Cbl mRNA according to data from the Immunological Genome Project.
source: Analysis of data from the Immunological Genome Project shows that mRNA expression of Lyn and c-Cbl are differentially regulated across different cell types. Mast cells, for instance, express very low levels of Cbl mRNA (Figure 8) (Heng and Painter, 2008; Dwyer et al., 2016), which translates into a low level of c-Cbl protein expression (Gustin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 8 and citations to prior literature.

claim: Low Cbl mRNA in mast cells translates into a low level of c-Cbl protein expression.
source: Analysis of data from the Immunological Genome Project shows that mRNA expression of Lyn and c-Cbl are differentially regulated across different cell types. Mast cells, for instance, express very low levels of Cbl mRNA (Figure 8) (Heng and Painter, 2008; Dwyer et al., 2016), which translates into a low level of c-Cbl protein expression (Gustin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and immunoblot data.

claim: Cblb mRNA is abundant in mast cells.
source: Cblb mRNA, in contrast, is abundant in mast cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Lyn is a key regulator of mast-cell ITAM signaling.
source: As in macrophages, Lyn is a key regulator of mast-cell ITAM signaling (Shelby et al., 2016), but the effect of disparate c-Cbl expression on LynA in the two cell types remains unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CskAS mast cells were homogeneous in their expression of the mast-cell markers FcεR1α and c-Kit (CD117).
source: CskAS mast cells were homogeneous in their expression of the mast-cell markers FcεR1α and c-Kit (CD117) (Kalesnikoff and Galli, 2011) (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Mast cells express very little c-Cbl (20% of the level in rested macrophages) and relatively high levels of Cbl-b (80% of the level in rested macrophages).
source: We then used immunoblotting to compare the expression of c-Cbl, Cbl-b, and LynA in CskAS mast cells and BMDMs and found that mast cells express very little c-Cbl (20% of the level in rested macrophages) and relatively high levels of Cbl-b (80% of the level in rested macrophages) (Figure 9B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Low c-Cbl expression in mast cells was accompanied by a complete resistance of LynA to degradation in the first 5 min of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: Strikingly, low c-Cbl expression was accompanied by a complete resistance of LynA to degradation in the first 5 min of 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Mast cells had increased steady-state expression of LynA (30% higher than in rested BMDMs).
source: Mast cells also had increased steady-state expression of LynA (30% higher than in rested BMDMs) (Figure 9E), despite low reported mRNA expression (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The combined effects of impaired degradation and increased steady-state expression resulted in 3-4x more LynA protein in mast cells than in rested BMDMs between 3 and 5 min of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
source: These combined effects resulted in 3-4x more LynA protein in mast cells than in rested BMDMs and 2x more than in primed BMDMs between 3 and 5 min of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from immunoblot data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Mast cells had a stronger signaling response to 3-IB-PP1 than macrophages.
source: Mast cells also had a stronger signaling response to 3-IB-PP1. Although the kinetics of Erk phosphorylation in mast cells varied, induction of pErk1/2 was consistently higher in mast cells than in macrophages, including in primed BMDMs (Figure 9F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Cell-specific expression of c-Cbl tunes the abundance of LynA protein at steady state and the half-life of that protein during activation.
source: We therefore hypothesized that cell-specific expression of c-Cbl tunes the abundance of LynA protein at steady state and the half-life of that protein during activation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparative data in macrophages and mast cells.

claim: Mast cells bypass the LynA signaling checkpoint by maintaining low levels of c-Cbl and therefore high levels of activated LynA.
source: Thus mast cells bypass the LynA signaling checkpoint by maintaining low levels of c-Cbl and therefore high levels of activated LynA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from data showing differential c-Cbl expression and LynA stability in mast cells.

claim: Transfection of saRNA into mast cells increased the expression of c-Cbl protein an average of 2-fold relative to mock-transfected cells.
source: Transfection of this saRNA into mast cells increased the expression of c-Cbl protein an average of 2-fold relative to mock-transfected cells (Figure 9G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 9.

claim: A modest increase in mast-cell c-Cbl expression increased LynA degradation in response to 3-IB-PP1 and suppressed downstream phosphorylation of Erk1/2.
source: Even this modest increase in mast-cell c-Cbl expression increased LynA degradation in response to 3-IB-PP1 and suppressed downstream phosphorylation of Erk1/2 (Figure 9I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 9.

claim: 3-IB-PP1 treatment for 15 min led to a 30% reduction of LynA protein in c-Cbl-overexpressing mast cells; LynA degradation at this time point was undetectable in control mast cells.
source: 3-IB-PP1 treatment for 15 min led to a 30% reduction of LynA protein in c-Cbl-overexpressing mast cells; LynA degradation at this time point was undetectable in control mast cells (Figure 9I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Erk1/2 phosphorylation was completely suppressed in mast cells treated with c-Cbl saRNA relative to control mast cells.
source: Correspondingly, Erk1/2 phosphorylation was completely suppressed in mast cells treated with c-Cbl saRNA relative to control mast cells (Figure 9J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Differential expression of c-Cbl in myeloid cells regulates the activation response of LynA, working together with transcriptional regulation to tune myeloid-cell responsiveness to SFK-mediated signaling.
source: Together, these data are consistent with a model in which differential expression of c-Cbl in myeloid cells regulates the activation response of LynA, working together with transcriptional regulation to tune myeloid-cell responsiveness to SFK-mediated signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the collective data in the manuscript.
